data.title: Zaggle up 7% from day's low on inking deal with Yokohama, WSFX Global Pay
data.description:
Zaggle Prepaid Ocean Services rebounded by 5.8 per cent from the day's low of ₹157.50 in Friday's intraday deals after the company announced signing a forex services agreement. The stock hit an intraday high of ₹168.18 on the NSE. At 1:45 PM, Zaggle pared gains and traded on a flat note at ₹162.67 on trades of around 40 lakh shares on the NSE. The stock hit a 52-week low at ₹146.65 on October 26, 2026, and a 52-week high of ₹397 was registered on November 28, 2025. Zaggle stock has witnessed a significant downturn since hitting a record high of ₹592 in September 2024. At current levels, the stock trades over 72 per cent lower compared to its peak, and down 53 per cent on a year-till-date basis. 

Zaggle inks 'Tripartite Agreement' with Yokohama and WSFX Global Pay

Zaggle Prepaid Ocean Services in an exchange filing on Friday, said the company entered into a tripartite agreement with Yokohama Private Limited (Customer) and WSFX Global Pay Limited (WSFX).

 According to the terms of the agreement, Zaggle shall provide Expense Management System (EMS) to Yokohama, while WSFX shall act as the Authorised Dealer for forex services to Yokohama. Revenue from the agreement is variable in nature, and shall be in force for one year, unless terminated earlier. "The Quantum of fees is subjected to the number of international transactions made by the employees of the customer for the respective months on the Platform. "In such a case it would be difficult to ascertain the value/amount of the contract at this stage," Zaggle said in its release. Vijay Kedia bought stake in August Kedia Securities, owned by veteran investor Vijay Kishanlal Kedia, acquired 20 lakh shares, representing a 1.48 per cent stake in Zaggle in August. Kedia bought 20 lakh equity shares at ₹164.72 per share, for an aggregate consideration of approximately ₹32.94 crore. Equirus Securities has 'Long' rating on Zaggle Equirus Securities has a 'Long' rating on Zaggle with a price target of ₹275 per share by March 2028. The brokerage said, Zaggle's Q2FY27 revenue execeded its estimate by 2.8 per cent, while Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization (Ebitda) was in line. Zaggle's management expects EBITDA margins of 7-8 per cent and continue to prioritise cash conversion and disciplined capitalisation. "Around 65-70 per cent of DICE contracts have been novated, with the remaining transfers expected in 3QFY27. We see Zaggle well positioned to benefit from wider adoption of spend management solutions, while acquisitions strengthen client stickiness," said the brokerage. Even as Equirus maintained a 'Long' rating, the brokerage cut FY27/FY28 earnings estimates by 13.4 per cent/6.2 per cent citing moderate programme fee growth and the near-term profitability drag from DICE integration. "We expect technology expenses, DICE integration and Zagg.money losses to weigh on near-term margins and model a 7.8 per cent EBITDA margin for FY27E,", the brocaded added. Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion.

data.title: India-US trade pact nears finish as pathway takes shape: Piyush Goyal
data.description:
The India-US trade deal is “close to culmination”, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Friday, indicating progress in negotiations days after Washington proposed a fresh tariff framework for Indian imports.
 
“The US trade deal is close to culmination. The process and pathway, which was always something which held back finalising the deal, is now taking some shape,” Goyal said while addressing the India Debt Capital Market Summit 2026 organised by TRUST Group.
 
His comments came after the US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods following a Section 301 investigation. Washington has indicated that the rate could be capped at 17 per cent if India and the US conclude a reciprocal trade agreement addressing the issues raised in the investigation.
 
 
India has disputed the US finding of structural excess capacity in its manufacturing industries and has said trade-related concerns should be addressed through bilateral trade negotiations.
 
Goyal also said the India-European Union free trade agreement was expected to be signed later this year and could come into effect by March or April 2027.
 
The minister said India's FTA coverage had expanded sharply over the past few years.
 
According to Goyal, before 2014, India's trade agreements covered economies with a combined gross domestic product (GDP) of about $10 trillion. Nine agreements finalised in the past four-and-a-half to five years, covering 38 developed countries, have added markets representing about $60 trillion of GDP.
 
Together, India's preferential market access now covers economies with around $70 trillion of GDP, he said.
 
Another eight or nine agreements under negotiation could add around $15 trillion, taking the total to about $85 trillion out of global GDP of $115-120 trillion, Goyal said.
 
“Almost every country in the world wants to do an FTA with India. We will add another $15 trillion. $85 trillion out of $115-120 trillion of global GDP will see India as a trusted partner; will see opportunities for India’s businesses to take forward,” he said.
 
On crude oil, Goyal said markets were sometimes too quick to re-rate or de-rate India based on relatively small movements in global prices.
 
While higher crude prices affected the economy, concerns that may have been significant in the 1990s or early 2000s needed to be viewed differently today given India's larger foreign exchange reserves, remittance flows, foreign direct investment and broader export base, he said.
 
“This could be an important matter of concern when we had much smaller foreign exchange reserves, much smaller remittances coming into the country, much less foreign direct investments coming into the country,” Goyal said.
 
A few dollars of movement in oil prices could not determine India's economic trajectory over the next two or three decades, he said, pointing to the country's expanding exports and economy.
 
The government said India had exported more than $700 billion annually and was targeting $1 trillion of goods and services exports in the current financial year.
 
Goyal also urged large companies, public sector undertakings and infrastructure developers to increasingly use the bond market as their first source of financing, including for long-duration capital expenditure.
 
He called for a broader investor base for long-term debt, asking insurers, pension and provident funds and mutual funds to increase participation in longer-duration instruments and look beyond only AAA-rated issuers.
 
The country's financing ecosystem would need to match the scale and duration of investments expected in areas such as semiconductor manufacturing, power grids, data centres and infrastructure over the coming decades, he said.
 
Goyal also urged exporters and their financiers to turn the market access created through FTAs into investment decisions by adding manufacturing capacity and preparing to serve newly opened markets.

data.title: 43 WTC wickets, 21.28 avg since Oval: Why is Siraj out of India's XI?
data.description:
When Jasprit Bumrah handed India's Test cap No. 321 to Gurnoor Brar at Hagley Oval on Friday morning, the moment captured the defining tension of the Gautam Gambhir coaching era. Out in the middle, a tall, raw fast bowler was being rewarded for a breakout white-ball tour with a dream red-ball debut on one of world cricket's premier seam-bowling decks. Beyond the boundary rope, wearing dark sunglasses as broadcast cameras lingered on him, stood Mohammed Siraj—India's leading wicket-taker in the 2025-27 World Test Championship, benched for a second consecutive overseas Test to end a six-year streak of playing in every away series since his 2020 debut.
 
 
Beside Siraj in the dugout sat Ravindra Jadeja, similarly overlooked for both Wellington and Christchurch. Thousands of kilometres away in Mumbai, wrist-spinner Kuldeep Yadav—originally named in the New Zealand Test squad—was bowling four-over spells for Uttar Pradesh against Mizoram in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy, having been released from the tour nearly two weeks earlier.
 
Across India's New Zealand assignment, Gambhir and captain Shubman Gill have pursued an unmistakably unsentimental blueprint: prioritize current rhythm over reputation, stretch batting depth deep into the lower order, and hand emerging fast bowlers real Test exposure in pace-friendly conditions. The result has ignited one of the sharpest selection debates in recent Indian cricket, pitting the long-term promise of a new pace crop against the jarring sight of proven match-winners being shown the exit.
 
The Siraj Data: What the numbers actually say
 
Nothing illustrates the debate better than the stark statistical split in Mohammed Siraj's career before and after his defining nine-wicket performance (4/86 and 5/104) at The Oval in August 2025, which sealed a six-run victory and a 2-2 series draw in England.
 
On the surface, dropping Siraj looks baffling. Far from declining after London, his overall output actually surged. Across the seven Tests following The Oval, Siraj claimed 21 wickets at an average of 21.28 and a strike rate of 44.3—a dramatic improvement on the seven Tests immediately preceding it (three in Australia, four in England), where he averaged 40.04 and struck every 58.4 balls. Even in home conditions, where pacers traditionally toil, his average dropped from 37.00 before The Oval (19 wickets in 14 Tests) to 20.23 afterward (17 wickets in five).

Dig deeper into the post-Oval window, however, and the reason behind the management's unease emerges. Siraj's seven Tests since London divide cleanly into two halves:
 
  • The 2025 peak: In four home Tests against the West Indies and South Africa between October and November 2025, Siraj was lethal—taking 16 wickets at 19.00 (SR 36.8), highlighted by 7/71 in Ahmedabad and 4/49 in Kolkata.
  • The 2026 stall: Across three Asian Tests in 2026—against Afghanistan in New Chandigarh and two Tests in Sri Lanka—his penetration dried up. He managed just five wickets at 28.60, needing 68.4 deliveries per breakthrough. In Sri Lanka specifically, he conceded just 2.34 runs an over across 44 overs, but took exactly one wicket in each of four innings (4 wickets, SR 66.0).
 
Crucially, his bowling volume had also contracted sharply—36.3% fewer deliveries across the seven post-Oval Tests (930 balls vs. 1,460 before), dropping from 34.8 overs per match to 22.1. After conceding 140 runs in 25 overs for South Zone in the Duleep Trophy final, Siraj diagnosed the issue not as fatigue from his 305.3-over workload under Gill, but as rust caused by long gaps between Tests. "I'm purely a rhythm bowler. If I'm not in sync, I simply can't explode through the crease. That was the struggle in Sri Lanka, my run-up felt disjointed," he admitted.
 
Yet even that explanation leaves the management's verdict open to scrutiny. At Hagley Oval itself in early November, Siraj looked back in sync, claiming 4/118 in 35 overs for India A against New Zealand A. Instead of getting another red-ball outing, he was flown to Mount Maunganui for the final ODI—where he dismissed Tim Seifert and Finn Allen—only to be told he was not at his "peak" when the Tests began. 
Cricket experts' push back: 'Where was Mohammed Siraj?'
 
That narrow 2026 subcontinental sample was nowhere near enough to convince former players and analysts that India should sideline a proven overseas workhorse in New Zealand—and the backlash only sharpened after the toss at Hagley Oval on Friday confirmed Siraj had been overlooked for a second consecutive Test.
 
Even from the opposition camp, the surprise was unmistakable. Speaking after the Christchurch toss, former New Zealand fast bowler Chris Martin admitted the hosts were relieved not to face him on a green seamers' track: "We are probably happy, from a New Zealand perspective, that Siraj is not playing, as he would've loved this pitch."
 
Earlier in the series, former India head coach Ravi Shastri had cut straight to the contradiction on X after Wellington: "If pace, skill and seam movement were the criteria, and 140 clicks was hard to come by, one has to ask the question. Where was MOHD SIRAJ? Experience, aggression and the ability to make things happen with the ball. Surely that counts for something!" Dinesh Karthik, speaking on Cricbuzz, likewise noted that Siraj's 2026 dip came entirely on flat subcontinental tracks: "He's shown that he's someone who can bowl really long spells. He can also bowl for 20-22 overs in a day. He's a workhorse and an absolute champion when it comes to the attitude that's required in Test matches." 
Mohammed Siraj stats. Source: Cricinfo
 
Once Gurnoor Brar was handed his debut cap ahead of Siraj in Christchurch, the post-toss criticism escalated across broadcast panels and social media:
  • Harsha Bhogle (on X) warned of the psychological message sent to India's pace group: "Siraj is now India's 6th ranked fast bowler. I find it so unfair. Of the top 5 wicket takers in test cricket in this WTC cycle, India now have place only for Bumrah. You wish the bowlers selected well, they have great conditions to bowl in, but they will know they won't get a long rope when it is their turn."
  • Ravichandran Ashwin, who had called the Wellington double omission of Siraj and Ravindra Jadeja "very harsh" and the "new normal," doubled down with pointed sarcasm on X during Day 1 in Christchurch. "While Akash Deep has been unplayable today, Siraj clearly looks like he has lost his bowling mojo. Hope he trains hard & tries to get back in time for the BGT," Ashwin wrote—before adding as New Zealand's middle order steadied late in the day: "This 60-80 over mark is usually the easiest time to bat & I hope Siraj can run in hard and get a breakthrough or two."
  • Mohammad Kaif (on X) questioned the mixed messaging from the camp: "Hard to believe as one of India's premier fast bowler Mohammed Siraj is dropped again. Siraj should be one of the first names considered in India's overseas Test bowling attack, alongside Bumrah. Interestingly, bowling coach Morne Morkel himself called Siraj a world-class bowler and said he was bowling well."
  • Murali Kartik (on Sony Sports) was visibly frustrated after broadcast cameras showed an emotional-looking Siraj walking near the boundary in sunglasses post-toss. "With the numbers you've seen so far, I am surprised. For what reason? Either don't keep him in the team at all then," Kartik fumed alongside Ajinkya Rahane. "If you feel his form isn't good, or he's not bowling well in the nets, or wherever, I don't know whatever the thinking might be, then don't take him on the tour at all. Don't take him; what's the point then?"
  • Sunil Gavaskar (on Sony Sports) broadened the post-toss critique to include Jadeja while ultimately choosing to rally behind the selected XI. "Well, we are only talking about Siraj, but what about Jadeja? He is India's third-highest wicket-taker in this WTC cycle. I do believe his spin would've been pretty useful on the fourth and fifth days... So, tough luck for him as well as Mohammed Siraj," Gavaskar said. "Now, Siraj is among the top wicket-takers in the cycle. So, let's wait and see. The way I've always seen it is that whatever reservations you might have about the XI, the 14 or the 16, once the team is selected, it is your team and my team. It's an Indian team. So, I back this team now that they've picked this playing XI, and I'm praying that this team does well."
 
The 'bowlers who can bat' doctrine and the Kuldeep Paradox
 
 Siraj's omission cannot be viewed in isolation. It sits inside a wider philosophical shift under Gambhir—one defined by batting depth, left-right matchups, and multi-skill utility players. Washington Sundar himself acknowledged earlier this year that Gambhir prefers packing the XI with all-rounders who can plug multiple roles.
 
In New Zealand, that philosophy reshaped both the spin and pace departments. Rather than pick pure strike bowlers, India opted for a tail that could bat: Anshul Kamboj (who struck a brisk 38 off 42 balls in India's massive 720/9 declared at Wellington), Akash Deep (13 off 5), and Washington Sundar (24 off 26) all helped extend the lower order.
 
The collateral damage was twofold. First, Ravindra Jadeja was left out for Sundar—a call that backfired on Day 5 in Wellington when New Zealand calmly batted out 120 overs for 239/5 to save the Test, with Sundar managing just 1/110 across 55 overs in the match. Former batter Subramaniam Badrinath summed up the flaw in prioritizing insurance over wicket-taking penetration: "Sundar didn't do anything wrong, but you have to win the Test match. Jadeja could have been the difference. Though you got 720 runs, you couldn't finish off the match. On Day 5, Jadeja could have easily been effective."
 
Second—and perhaps most tellingly—was the BCCI's November 14 decision to release Kuldeep Yadav from the Test squad to play domestic cricket back home while drafting in Gurnoor Brar. Kuldeep boasts a Test bowling average of 23.36 and a strike rate of 39.38 across 19 matches, yet averages 12.60 with the bat.
 
New Zealand leg-spinner Ish Sodhi, speaking to PTI ahead of the Christchurch Test, laid bare the brutal math working against specialist wrist-spinners in Gambhir's setup: "Kuldeep is competing in those conditions with guys like Washington Sundar and Ravindra Jadeja, who both average 40 with the bat, if not more, in Test cricket. I can understand it from a selection point of view. From an emotional point of view, it sucks."
 
Former India captain Sourav Ganguly was far less forgiving after India failed to bowl New Zealand out in Wellington, taking to X to challenge the blurring of roles: "Washington can play as an allrounder ..@bcci where is Kuldeep or Manav Suthar?"
 
The counter-argument: Why Gambhir's youth gamble matters
 
For all the legitimate criticism of how senior match-winners have been handled, dismissing Gambhir's New Zealand strategy as mere T20-style tinkering misses an equally important reality: Indian Test cricket has historically struggled to blood young fast bowlers in forgiving seam conditions before they are thrown into the cauldron of Australia or England.
 
Gambhir has repeatedly championed the value of bowling attacks developed on sporting pitches—posting "Bowlers win you series!" after India's young pace unit engineered a historic ODI series triumph in New Zealand earlier this month. Carrying that conviction into the Test series meant trusting Akash Deep, Anshul Kamboj, Prasidh Krishna, and Gurnoor Brar on tracks where pace actually has a voice. At Hagley Oval, fast bowlers had accounted for 444 of 484 Test wickets (91.7%) across 15 Tests heading into Friday.
 
And the young quicks have offered genuine glimpses of why the management is investing in them:
 
  • Akash Deep was India's most disciplined seamer in Wellington (3/53 in the first innings) and carried that control into Christchurch, taking two wickets on Day 1 by dismissing Tom Latham (59) and Rachin Ravindra (0). 
  • Gurnoor Brar, rewarded for his ODI Player of the Series form and praised by teammates for his character, generated steep bounce on debut at Hagley Oval and claimed Devon Conway (31) on the stroke of lunch for his maiden Test wicket. 
  • Anshul Kamboj, though inconsistent with the new ball in Christchurch, chipped in with Henry Nicholls' wicket (16) on Day 1, building on his two wickets and vital lower-order runs in Wellington. 
  • Prasidh Krishna, despite enduring a tough first innings in Wellington (1/100), bounced back with 2/23 in the second innings before making way for Brar's fresh legs on a three-day turnaround.
 
Even with Jasprit Bumrah going wicketless on Day 1 in Christchurch and Washington Sundar removing Daryl Mitchell, India's restructured attack kept New Zealand in check through a strong middle session before Tom Blundell (53*) and Glenn Phillips (36*) steered the hosts to 246/5 in 85 overs at stumps.

data.title: EPF account inactive for 3 years? Know when interest stops and how to claim
data.description:
An account with no fresh contributions does not automatically stop earning interest after three years. The rules depend on the member's age and circumstances.
 
An Employees' Provident Fund (EPF) account does not automatically become inoperative if no contributions have been credited for three years. For employees who leave a job before turning 55, their accumulated provident fund savings can continue to earn interest until they turn 58, subject to the applicable rules.
 
The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) has recently urged subscribers to check whether their accounts have become inoperative and understand the rules governing interest accrual, withdrawals and transfers. Its communication on November 24 also directed members to an explanatory video on the subject.
 
 
The clarification is important for employees who switch jobs, take a career break or leave the workforce, as they may mistakenly believe their old PF account has stopped earning interest after three years.
 

When does an EPF account become inoperative?

Under the EPF rules, an account is classified as inoperative in specific circumstances, rather than simply because contributions have stopped for three years.
 
These include:
 
Retirement after 55: If a member retires after attaining 55 years and does not claim the balance within 36 months, the account can become inoperative.
 
Permanent migration abroad: An account can become inoperative if the member permanently settles abroad and does not claim the money within the prescribed period.
 
Death of a member: If nominees or legal heirs do not claim the accumulated amount within 36 months.
 
Failed payment: If a settlement amount is returned because of incorrect or outdated bank details and remains unclaimed for 36 months.
 
The rules governing inoperative accounts are laid down under the EPF Scheme. The EPFO has clarified that interest on an operative account can continue until the member turns 58, subject to applicable provisions.
 

Does an inoperative account mean your money is lost?

 
No. An inoperative account does not mean the accumulated PF money is forfeited.
 
The balance remains claimable after the member completes the required verification and submits the appropriate application. However, interest is not credited once an account becomes inoperative.
 
Members should therefore avoid leaving their PF savings unattended, particularly if they have changed jobs and have not transferred their accumulated balance.
 
How to withdraw or transfer your PF balance
Members can access their EPF savings through the EPFO Member e-Sewa portal. Before filing a claim, they should check whether their Aadhaar, bank account details and other KYC information are updated and verified.
 

The process involves the following steps:

 
Withdraw the balance: Submit Form 19 online through the EPFO portal for final settlement, subject to eligibility.
 
Transfer the balance: If you have joined another EPF-covered employer, submit Form 13 to transfer the accumulated savings to the new PF account instead of withdrawing them.
 
Claim after death: Nominees or legal heirs can submit the applicable claim forms, including Form 20, subject to the relevant rules.
 
Transferring the balance when changing jobs can help maintain continuity in retirement savings and preserve the benefits associated with long-term EPF accumulation.
 
Members can log in to the EPFO Member e-Sewa portal using their Universal Account Number (UAN) and password to check their balance, update details and initiate claims.
 
The first step for anyone with an old PF account should be to check the balance and account details before deciding whether to withdraw or transfer the money.

data.title: IIFCL, UCO Bank eye debut dollar debt before RBI window shuts, say bankers
data.description:
State-run financiers India Infrastructure Finance Company (IIFCL) and UCO Bank plan to ​issue debut dollar-denominated bonds next month before the central bank's subsidised swap window closes, two merchant bankers said on Friday.
 
The plans come as US Treasury yields slide amid an unravelling of the global AI trade and investors ‌flocking towards safe-haven assets, making the window, ​which closes on December 31, ​more attractive.
 
IIFCL could raise around $500 million through a five-year debt issue, ​while UCO Bank could add to the $1 billion fundraising it has already approved with a smaller size of around $250 million-$300 million maturing in three or five years, the bankers said.
 
 
The bankers requested anonymity ​as the matters are still private, while IIFCL and UCO Bank ‌did not reply to Reuters emails for comments.
 
Some Indian firms had ​earlier pushed back their plans after a spike in Treasury yields made borrowing more expensive, the bankers said.
 
IIFCL recently held meetings with investors as part ‌of a non-deal road show ​and received a BBB long-term ‌rating from S&P earlier this month.
 
The debt of UCO Bank is ‌rated BBB by S&P and BBB- by Fitch Ratings.
 
In June, the ​Reserve Bank of India announced measures to stabilise the rupee, including a subsidised hedging facility for lenders and state-run ​firms to lower their overall borrowing costs.
 
Indian lenders have so far raised $13 billion under the scheme.
 
In September, National ‌Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development raised dollar debt worth $750 million through 10-year ‌papers at 6.1220%, or at a spread of 105 basis points above comparable US yields.
 
Power Finance Corp also raised $300 million through three-year bonds at a spread of 110 bps over US Treasuries.

data.title: Glenmark Pharma hits new high, up 5th straight day; gains 35% from Oct low
data.description:
Glenmark Pharmaceuticals share price movement

 
Glenmark Pharmaceuticals’ share price hit a new high of ₹2,846, rallying 4 per cent on the BSE in Friday’s intraday deals in an otherwise weak market due to better business outlook. In comparison, the BSE Sensex was down 0.84 per cent at 83,624 at 01:07 PM.
 
The stock price of the pharma company quoted higher for the fifth straight day, surging 9 per cent. It bounced back 35 per cent from its previous month low of ₹2,103 touched on October 23, 2026.
 

Glenmark Pharma – Q2 results

 
On a like-for-like basis, Glenmark Pharma said consolidated revenue grew approximately 20 per cent year-on-year (YoY). Its India formulations business recorded revenue of ₹1,327 crore, growing 14 per cent, while North America revenue stood at ₹1,209 crore. Excluding deferred out-licensing income recognition for ISB 2001, the core North American business grew approximately 31 per cent. Europe revenue increased 6.2 per cent to ₹792 crore, while emerging markets revenue grew 33.2 per cent to ₹877 crore.
 
 
Glenn Saldanha, chairman and managing director of Glenmark Pharmaceuticals, said the company remained on track to deliver its FY27 guidance, supported by continued growth in India, a recovery in North America and robust performance in emerging markets.
 
The company expects the first launch from its partnered innovative oncology pipeline by the end of FY27. Its innovation arm, Ichnos Glenmark Innovation, is also advancing its multispecific oncology pipeline, with Phase I data for ISB 2001 selected for an oral presentation at the 2026 American Society of Hematology Annual Meeting.
 
Glenmark's India formulation business recorded a growth of 16.7 per cent in the second quarter and 15.7 per cent as per moving annual total (MAT) September 2026 data, compared to the Indian Pharmaceutical Market (IPM) growth of 13.8 per cent in Q2 and 12.1 per cent in MAT September. Glenmark continues to sustain strong growth in its core therapeutic areas like dermatology, respiratory, cardiac, and oncology.
 
As the operating leverage kicks in H2FY27, the management expects gross debt to be zero by end of FY27. The company remains focused on the prudent capital allocation, and accordingly, the management said the company is focusing on its strategic growth targets and maintaining healthy balance sheet ratios.  Check - TOP GAINERS NSE | TOP LOSERS NSE 

Motilal Oswal Financial Services view on Glenmark Pharma

 
Glenmark Pharma delivered a better-than-expected operational performance in Q2FY27, with a 5 per cent beat on revenue/ earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA). Earnings were largely in line as the impact of higher-than-expected EBITDA was offset by lower other income, analysts at Motilal Oswal Financial Services said.
 
On a like-to-like basis, Glenmark Pharma outperformed the industry in the domestic formulation segment by almost 300bp for the quarter, backed by superior execution in cardiology, dermatology and respiratory segments. It continued to launch differentiated oncology, respiratory as well as dermatology products, supporting better growth prospects in the domestic formulation (DF) segment, the brokerage firm said.
 
The strategic reset in DF and new launches in North America has led to improved performance and a better outlook going forward. The clinical development related to innovative oncology and immunology molecules is progressing on track. Also, the company intends to be gross debt zero by FY27, strengthening the balance sheet, the brokerage firm said, as it maintains a 'Buy' rating on the stock with a target price of ₹3,000 per share. Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion.

data.title: Strobe Talbott, architect of India-US ties post-Pokhrann-II, passes away
data.description:
Former US diplomat Strobe Talbott, who along with the then External Affairs Minister Jaswant Singh, played a key role in bridging the chasm between the US and India after the 1998 Pokhran nuclear tests, breathed his last.

Talbott, the former US Deputy Secretary of State under President Bill Clinton, passed away at his home in East Hampton, New York on Thursday after a long illness, his son Devin Talbott said. He was 80.

Caught off guard by India's five nuclear tests on May 11 and May 13, 1998, the US imposed sanctions on New Delhi and it was the Talbott-Singh duo who held a series of meetings over the next two years to put the bilateral relationship between the estranged democracies back on track.

 

Their 14 meetings in seven countries across three continents laid the groundwork for President Clinton's visit to India in 2000. This was the first visit by a US president to India in 22 years which helped end fifty years of estrangement between the world's two largest democracies.

The Talbott-Singh talks also laid the foundation for a civil nuclear agreement between India and the US, thus ending New Delhi's long nuclear winter.

During his discussions with Singh, Talbott underscored five "benchmarks" on India sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), halt production of fissile material, show restraint in deploying missiles and warheads, tighten export controls, and resume dialogue with Pakistan.

Talbott wanted a time-frame set for producing substantial results from the dialogue, but Singh managed to turn these ideas away without antagonising his American interlocutor.

"By weathering the storm of US disapproval - by outlasting and outtalking the Americans in the marathon of diplomacy spurred by the test, in short, by not compromising - the Indians would prove their resolve and their resilience, thereby giving a boost to their national self-esteem and self-confidence," Talbott wrote in his book Engaging India: Diplomacy, Democracy and the Bomb'.

"As one of the architects of the Indian strategy, Jaswant Singh came closer to achieving his objective in the dialogue than I did to achieving mine," the American journalist-turned-diplomat said about his two-and-a-half years long discussions with Singh.

Born in Dayton, Ohio in 1946, Talbott was a journalist at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist.

Talbott joined the US State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries.

Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the US State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

data.title: Over 500 cops deployed for Diljit's Mumbai concert after bomb threat
data.description:
More than 500 Mumbai police personnel will be deployed at Mahalaxmi Racecourse here for actor-singer Diljit Dosanjh's concert on Friday following a threat email warning of possible attacks on the venue and Metro stations, officials said.

Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad (BDDS) teams have swept the venue, they said, adding that entry checks will be carried out across all five gates instead of three.

Private security personnel have also been roped in to assist police, an official said.

An email threatening blasts, grenade attacks and planting of IEDs at the mayor's office, metro rail stations and Dosanjh's concert was received on Thursday, the anniversary of the devastating 26/11 terror attacks.

 

The email, sent by an individual identifying herself as Hannah Meler, contained references to Khalistan, the 1984 anti-Sikh riots as well as threats of violence linked to a programme involving Dosanjh and people associated with the event.

In view of the threat, the Mumbai police has deployed around 200 constables, 150 women constables and 75 officers, besides plainclothes personnel stationed around the singer. Dog squads and an Anti-Narcotics Cell (ANC) team will also remain present at the venue, an official said.

He said that a no-car zone extending 500 to 700 metres around the racecourse will be enforced, and parking will not be permitted at the event, though no road diversions have been announced.

Organisers have been instructed not to disclose details of the singer's hotel or arrival time as part of the security protocol, sources said.

Meanwhile, organisers have prohibited posters, banners, signs and flags of any kind inside Mahalaxmi Racecourse for the concert, which is part of Dosanjh's RuPay AURA India Tour 2026.

data.title: 3rd earnings upgrade in 2 decades: Jefferies lists stocks to play the trend
data.description:
Fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) is trending differently, as India Inc. is set for its rare earnings upgrade. According to global investment bank Jefferies, MSCI India earnings estimates have historically been revised lower through the year, with downgrades in 18 of the past 20 completed fiscal years.
 
This time, Jefferies upgraded earnings per share (EPS) estimates by 1 per cent compared to the start of the fiscal year, making it only the third upgrade year in two decades, after FY12 (+1 per cent) and FY24 (+2 per cent). Economic growth has been revenue supportive, and we believe 4-year low margins could provide earnings support ahead.  
 
 
This, the brokerage said, is notable against an average c.10 per cent downgrade over FY07-26.  
 
"Revenue growth for Jefferies coverage ex-O&G/metals/financials accelerated for the fifth consecutive quarter to 21 per cent YoY in Sep’26, a 15-quarter high. This supported 19 per cent YoY earnings growth ex-O&G/metals despite EBITDA margins being near four-year lows. Going forward, while revenue growth may not accelerate further, we believe that margin improvements can provide support to earnings growth," Abhinav Sinha, along with other analysts, wrote in the Equity Strategy note shared on November 26.
 

Stocks to play upgrade cycle

Among sectors, the positive revisions within Jefferies coverage have been led by banks and non-banking finance companies (NBFCs), with 73 per cent and 71 per cent of stocks seeing FY27E EPS upgrades post Sep’26 results, while cyclical commodities (O&G, Metals) have also seen broad upgrades. 
ALSO READ: Stock Market LIVE: Sensex slumps 700 pts, Nifty below 25,700; Auto, IT down 1% each
 
Among stocks seeing consistent upgrades over the past two quarters, our preferred names include ICICI Bank, Kotak Bank, SBI, Bajaj Finance, Lodha, Lenskart, and Indian Hotels, said the investment bank. Reliance Industries and JSW Steel also stand out as preferred names where revision momentum has recently turned positive, it added.
 
On the flip side, Cement, Autos and IT saw higher downgrades post Sep’26 results. Among stocks with persistent downgrades over the past two quarters, where we have an Underperform rating, are LTM, Hyundai, Indus Towers, Tata Motors, TCS and Wipro, Jefferies noted.
 

Edge over EM peers

Jefferies also noted that India ranks first against its emerging market (EM) peers on earnings framework, as the potential slowdown in AI capex poses downside risks to Korea and Taiwan.
 
"While India’s EPS growth trails EM ex-AI majors (Samsung, SK hynix and TSMC) by 19ppt in CY26E/FY27E, it is expected to move to a 3ppt lead in CY27E/FY28E, pointing to an improving relative earnings outlook," it said.
